label: Lagrangian Submanifolds
notes: This lecture covers printed pages 13 through 19. We meet Lagrangian submanifolds, the half-dimensional submanifolds on which the symplectic form restricts to zero. The recurring theme is that every Lagrangian test reduces to pulling back a form and checking that it vanishes, turning geometry into differential identities.

label: Submanifolds and Pullbacks
notes: Before testing Lagrangians we fix submanifold language. An immersion injects tangent vectors, an embedding fixes the topology, and a closed embedding gives the submanifolds used here. Every later test is a pullback: restrict the tautological one-form or the symplectic form to the candidate and read whether it dies on tangent vectors.

label: The Lagrangian Condition
notes: A Lagrangian submanifold is isotropic and half-dimensional: the restricted symplectic form vanishes and the dimension is exactly n inside the two-n manifold. Isotropy alone forces dimension at most n, so Lagrangians are the maximal isotropic submanifolds. Numerically the residual matrix B transpose Omega B must be the zero matrix.

label: Cotangent Bundle and Tautological Form
notes: On the cotangent bundle the tautological one-form alpha is defined point by point, and omega equals minus d alpha. The zero section and the individual cotangent fibers are the first Lagrangians. Both have dimension n, and alpha restricts to zero on each, so the canonical two-form restricts to zero as well.

label: Graphs of One-Forms
notes: A one-form mu is a section of the cotangent bundle whose image is its graph. The key computation is that pulling the tautological form back along the section returns mu itself. Therefore pulling omega back returns minus d mu, and the graph is Lagrangian exactly when mu is closed. This is the heart of the lecture.

label: Closed Versus Exact
notes: The graph criterion links Lagrangians to de Rham cohomology. Closed one-forms give Lagrangian graphs; on a simply connected base every closed form is exact, mu equals df. Then the generating function f produces the Lagrangian, and intersections of the graph with the zero section are exactly the critical points of f.

label: A Worked Graph Test
notes: We make the criterion concrete in two dimensions. The gradient one-form of a radial potential is closed, so its graph is Lagrangian; the rotational one-form minus y dx plus x dy has constant nonzero exterior derivative, so its graph fails. The same coefficient that measures d mu measures the pullback of omega, side by side.

label: The Conormal Bundle
notes: Given a submanifold S of the base, the conormal bundle collects covectors that annihilate the tangent space of S. In coordinates adapted to S, tangent motion has no normal differential and conormal covectors have no tangent component. Both facts together make the tautological form vanish, so the conormal bundle is Lagrangian and has dimension n.

label: The Twisted Product
notes: To compare two symplectic manifolds we form their product and twist the form by subtracting the second factor: pr-one-star omega-one minus pr-two-star omega-two. This twisted form is symplectic on the product. It is the arena in which maps between the two manifolds become submanifolds, namely their graphs sitting inside the product.

label: Symplectomorphisms as Lagrangians
notes: The graph of a diffeomorphism phi is Lagrangian for the twisted product form exactly when phi is a symplectomorphism. Pulling the twisted form back over the graph yields omega-one minus phi-star omega-two, whose vanishing is precisely the symplectomorphism condition. This is the symplectic creed: everything is a Lagrangian submanifold.

label: Recap and the Creed
notes: We collected the canonical Lagrangians: the zero section, the fibers, graphs of closed one-forms, conormal bundles, and graphs of symplectomorphisms. Each was certified by a single vanishing pullback. Carry forward the slogan that turning maps into Lagrangian graphs lets submanifold techniques solve problems about symplectomorphisms.
